name: Stressors and Stress Responses
what: This subtopic covers the definition of stress and stressors, the distinction between internal and external stressors, psychological stress responses including eustress and distress, and the two key physiological stress responses: the flight-or-fight-or-freeze response in acute stress and the role of cortisol in chronic stress.
why: Understanding how stressors are categorised and how the body and mind respond helps explain why different people experience stress differently and why certain physiological reactions occur. This foundational knowledge underpins all subsequent models studied in this topic.

items.title: I can distinguish between a stressor and stress
items.what: A stressor is the stimulus (internal or external) that triggers the stress response. Stress is the psychological and physiological experience that results from encountering something that demands attention or coping effort.
items.why: Using these terms correctly is required in exam responses. Confusing them is a common error that costs marks, and precise language reflects accurate conceptual understanding.
items.example: An upcoming psychology exam is the stressor. The worry, increased heart rate, and difficulty sleeping that follow are the stress response.

items.title: I can distinguish between internal and external stressors and give examples of each
items.what: Internal stressors originate from within the person and include cognitive and biological factors such as negative attitude, rumination, low self-esteem, and nervous system dysfunction (e.g. low GABA). External stressors originate from the environment, such as exams, financial difficulty, or arguments with others.
items.why: This distinction is directly tested and helps explain why two people in the same situation can experience very different levels of stress. Internal stressors shape how external events are perceived.
items.example: A student sitting an exam (external stressor) repeatedly tells themselves they will fail (rumination, an internal stressor), amplifying their stress beyond what the exam alone would produce.

items.title: I can explain the difference between eustress and distress as psychological stress responses
items.what: Eustress is a form of stress characterised by a positive psychological state, involving emotions such as excitement and motivation. Distress is a form of stress characterised by a negative psychological state, involving emotions such as worry and frustration. Both demonstrate the subjective nature of stress.
items.why: Recognising that stress is not always negative is important for understanding why the same stressor can produce different responses in different individuals. Eustress can actually enhance performance.
items.example: Two students are told they have been selected to represent the school at a debate. One feels motivated and excited (eustress); the other feels overwhelmed and dreads the event (distress).

items.title: I can describe the flight-or-fight-or-freeze response as a physiological response to acute stress
items.what: Acute stress is intense and brief. The flight-or-fight-or-freeze response is an involuntary, automatic reaction to an immediate threat. Flight and fight involve sympathetic nervous system activation and adrenaline release. Freeze involves a brief parasympathetic activation causing immobility, followed by sympathetic activation.
items.why: This response explains why the body reacts so rapidly to immediate danger. Understanding the role of the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems in each component is required for exam questions.
items.example: A student is unexpectedly called on to answer a question in class. They may feel a surge of energy and speak up (fight), feel the urge to leave the room (flight), or go blank and be unable to respond (freeze).

items.title: I can explain the role of cortisol in chronic stress
items.what: Chronic stress endures for several months or longer. Cortisol is a hormone released by the adrenal glands that helps maintain heightened arousal over this extended period. In the short term it increases blood sugar, improves metabolism, energises the body, and reduces inflammation. With prolonged elevation, cortisol suppresses the immune system.
items.why: Cortisol explains the biological mechanism behind long-term stress effects including increased susceptibility to illness. It also links lesson 3A content to Selye's GAS model studied in lesson 3B.
items.example: A student under exam pressure for an entire school year has sustained elevated cortisol. By late in the year they develop frequent colds as their immune system has been chronically suppressed.

items.title: I can compare psychological and physiological stress responses
items.what: Psychological stress responses (eustress and distress) are subjective, varying between individuals experiencing the same stressor. Physiological stress responses (such as the fight-or-flight-or-freeze response and cortisol release) are largely objective, occurring in similar ways across different people.
items.why: This comparison is a recurring exam question type. Understanding the subjective versus objective distinction is essential for correctly applying these concepts to novel scenarios.
items.example: Two people watch the same horror film. Both experience increased heart rate (similar physiological response), but one finds it thrilling (eustress) while the other finds it deeply unsettling (distress).
